meta.title: Whisper quantization WER degradation curve
meta.question: What INT quantization level produces the first statistically significant WER degradation in Whisper vs FP16 on clean speech?

pitch.one_line_answer: INT8 is near-lossless on clean speech (Q8_0 WER 4.73% vs F16 4.94%, p=0.38, 47% smaller) — but so is INT4: Q4_0 WER 5.15% vs 4.94% (+4.2%, p=0.57, not significant) and 71% smaller. The predicted degradation cliff does not exist on LibriSpeech test-clean.
pitch.elevator: The received wisdom: quantizing Whisper below FP16 hurts transcription accuracy, so pick the highest bit-width you can afford. This project measured the actual degradation curve on LibriSpeech test-clean with a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test — and found no statistically significant WER penalty even at INT4. large-v3 resists quantization far better than predicted on clean speech; the size savings are real (71% at Q4_0) and the accuracy cost, on this corpus, is not measurable.

hypotheses.statement: Under LibriSpeech test-clean conditions, INT4-quantized Whisper large-v3 shows statistically significant WER degradation (p <= 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank) and >10% relative WER increase vs FP16 baseline.
Under LibriSpeech test-clean conditions, INT8-quantized Whisper large-v3 shows no statistically significant WER degradation vs FP16 (p > 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank), with relative WER increase < 5%.

headline.text: Q4_0: WER 5.15% vs F16 4.94% (+4.2% relative, p=0.57) — not statistically significant, crossing neither the 10% nor the p<=0.05 falsification thresholds
Q8_0: WER 4.73% vs F16 4.94% (-4.2% relative, p=0.38) — near-lossless on large-v3 clean speech

journey.title: Two hypotheses, one pipeline
journey.summary: The literature gave the falsifier a shape: INT4 degradation would have to be statistically significant (p<=0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank) AND exceed 10% relative WER increase to matter; INT8 was expected to be near-lossless. Two hypotheses fixed both sides of the curve before any measurement existed.

journey.title: The pipeline was verified before it was trusted
journey.summary: The whisper.cpp WER pipeline was proven end-to-end with tiny.en first (E-004) — transcription, WER computation, and the statistical test — so a surprising result could not be blamed on broken machinery.

journey.title: The degradation cliff was not there
journey.summary: 100 random LibriSpeech test-clean samples, paired per-sample WER: Q4_0 5.15% vs F16 4.94% (+4.2%, p=0.57); Q8_0 4.73% (-4.2%, p=0.38). H-001's falsification condition met in the negative — INT4 shows no significant degradation on clean speech — and H-002 supported: INT8 is near-lossless. The honest headline: the expected cliff is absent, and the safe claim is 'INT8 near-lossless', because that was the hypothesis that survived.

lessons: Clean speech is the easiest case for quantization — the result is strongest where degradation is least likely. The interesting measurement is noisy speech, and this corpus does not cover it; that gap is the most valuable next step.

Verifying the pipeline on a small model (tiny.en) before the expensive large-v3 run separated machinery errors from surprising results — the falsified hypothesis would have been far less credible otherwise.
Writing two hypotheses (one expected to fail, one expected to hold) turned a partial result into a complete answer: both halves of the degradation curve are covered by pre-registered claims.

limitations.baseline_wins: The baseline was never beaten, nor was it supposed to be: FP16 remains the reference accuracy. What changed is the knowledge of how much accuracy lower precisions give up — on clean speech, a statistically undetectable amount.
limitations.untested: 100 random test-clean samples only; LibriSpeech test-other (noisy speech) was not run. Non-English corpora untested. The statistical power at n=100 bounds the detectable degradation — a sub-4% real penalty could hide below it.
limitations.next_level: To extend the curve: run the same paired test on test-other, where degradation is expected to appear first, and increase n for tighter confidence intervals. That is a new measurement, not more of this one.
limitations.structural: whisper.cpp quantization levels (Q8_0, Q4_0) are the ggml schemes, not all INT variants; results do not transfer to other runtimes. The 95% CI for Q4_0 is [3.49%, 7.00%] — the claim 'no degradation' holds only within that band.

audience.who_is_this_for: Engineers choosing a whisper.cpp quantization level for memory-constrained deployments on clean speech — this is the measured trade-off table between size and WER they currently have to guess at.
audience.not_for: Anyone deploying on noisy or multilingual audio, where these numbers do not apply — this repository says so explicitly rather than letting the clean-speech result overgeneralise.
